issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: For a rape trauma profile, the appraisal 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' is the only item that implies perpetration or morally troubling behaviour by the patient. Paired with memory items centered on terror and shame and trigger items tied to tiredness, driving with others, and sounds, this appraisal is hard to reconcile clinically with the rest of the profile and with the trauma type. The other negative appraisals reflect mistrust and loss of faith, which fit sexual assault trauma; this item instead points toward a different moral injury formulation and creates an internal mismatch within the Negative Appraisals node.

vignette: David Rossi, fifty-three, had spent nearly two decades navigating the city’s transit routes until his routine fractured on a rain-slicked Tuesday night. He had been on his final run, his body already heavy with the kind of bone-deep exhaustion that made his eyelids feel like lead and his reflexes sluggish. When a lone man boarded at the terminus, David tried to maintain his professional composure, but the weight of his fatigue made him lower his guard. Within minutes, the man had pinned him against the driver’s partition, his grip unrelenting as David’s struggle yielded to paralysis. The assault was accompanied by the hiss of the hydraulic doors sealing them in, the sharp metallic clank of the fare box, and the attacker’s ragged breathing. That night, the perfect storm of his depleted energy, the inescapable proximity of another person, and the specific acoustic signature of the bus transformed a routine shift into a violation that left him trembling long after the engine was cut. In the weeks that followed, David’s attempts to return to the road only sharpened his distress. When he felt that familiar exhaustion creeping into his shoulders on a long stretch of highway, or when the rhythm of traffic placed passengers in his mirrors, the memories of the assault would surge forward with unwavering force. He would catch himself gripping the wheel until his knuckles blanched, his mind instantly transported back to the driver’s seat, replaying the scene in a relentless loop that felt less like a recollection and more like a live broadcast. Those moments of sensory overload did not merely summon the past; they fundamentally reshaped how he viewed the world and himself. Each time the bus doors hissed or a fare payer leaned too close, David’s mind automatically wired those cues to a new, grim certainty: people could not be trusted, and life had stripped away any remaining faith in safety or divine order. The physical toll of the encounter left him with a profound sense of body shame, as though his own flesh had become a site of betrayal rather than protection. The terror and shame that flooded his system on recall quickly became self-perpetuating. David found that his deepening mistrust and the heavy shame he carried about his body acted as a cognitive filter, ensuring that ordinary auditory cues—a sudden brake screech, a passenger’s cough, the low hum of an idling engine—now triggered vivid, unbidden memories of the attack. Conversely, the more violently those replayed memories intruded, the more they sharpened his physiological alarm, pulling the triggers of human proximity and everyday sound into unbearable focus. This internal loop tightened relentlessly over the months. His conviction that people were inherently dangerous and that his own body was compromised kept him constantly braced, which funneled directly back into his avoidance behaviors. He started taking unscheduled breaks, parking the bus in secluded industrial lots to wait out shifts, and avoiding routes that required prolonged interaction with commuters. His marriage, once a source of stability, now felt strained by his withdrawal; he would flinch when his wife reached for his arm and would isolate himself in the garage rather than sit in the living room, convinced that proximity only invited harm. The cycle reinforced itself without pause: his negative appraisals amplified his sensitivity to fatigue and sound, which pulled the memories forward, and the replayed terror and shame made every ordinary moment feel like a prelude to violence. By the time David finally walked into the clinic, the weight of this loop had collapsed his professional standing and left him emotionally depleted. It was his wife’s quiet despair over his sudden aversion to sharing meals and his constant state of physical tension that finally pushed him to seek treatment. His structured assessment returned a PCL-5 score of 76, reflecting the severe intrusion and hyperarousal that had colonized his days. He sat in the intake chair with his shoulders drawn inward, his voice low as he described how he could no longer distinguish between past and present, how the hum of the waiting room’s HVAC system made his chest tighten with the same paralysis he felt years ago. What he feared most was that the shame and mistrust had permanently broken his ability to trust his own judgment or feel safe in his own skin. Yet, beneath the exhaustion, there was a fragile hope that someone might help him untangle the threads that had bound his triggers, memories, and beliefs into a prison from which he no longer saw an exit.
